source.title: Generative AI and Large Language Models for Cyber Security: All Insights You Need
source.authors: M. Ferrag; Fatima Alwahedi; A. Battah; Bilel Cherif; Abdechakour Mechri; Norbert Tihanyi

page_placements.theme: Post-training changes capabilities at fixed model size

record.file_problem: The full text is present. The title supplied in the request differs from the title printed in the paper; the paper title is “Generative AI in Cybersecurity: A Comprehensive Review of LLM Applications and Vulnerabilities.”
record.tranche_reason: The survey reports its own downstream cybersecurity evaluations across models of different stated sizes and comments on the size–performance relationship. This is a different measure from pretraining loss or a controlled scaling-law sweep, and it does not test the original scaling-law recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit or test power laws, compare small-run fits with much larger runs, or measure compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its own CyberMetric and hardware-security evaluations bear on V6; the rows record the 10,000-question CyberMetric results and hardware bug-detection results. Scaling-law descriptions, model results attributed to cited work, and the CyberMetric results at 80, 500, and 2,000 questions are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The authors report their own cybersecurity evaluations across model sizes and explicitly assess the size–performance relationship. These results bear on V6 in a new downstream setting, although they do not establish a predictive scaling function. V1–V5 and V7 are only discussed or left untested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report heterogeneous cybersecurity capabilities, little association between model size and hardware bug detection/CWE identification, and exceptions to larger models performing better on CyberMetric. They call for larger, more dedicated hardware evaluations before conclusive findings. They do not conclude anything about pretraining-loss power laws.
record.recipe_differences: The paper is a cybersecurity review with cross-model downstream task evaluations, not a reproduction of a scaling-law loss fit or compute-allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies by evaluated model and task. CyberMetric scores are also reported for multiple question-set sizes, but those results are not extracted here.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed stated size, instruction tuning substantially changes CyberMetric accuracy: Mistral-7B base 39.28% versus instruct-v0.1 67.29%, and Llama-3-8B base 36.00% versus instruct 71.25%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptation and instruction tuning can strongly affect cybersecurity benchmark accuracy at fixed parameter count. These contrasts do not measure V4 architecture effects or V7 fitted-law dependence.

record.problems: The evaluations compare heterogeneous models rather than controlled scale variants; they do not report pretraining loss or compute, and the paper gives no uncertainty estimates. The supplied text has inconsistencies in model counts (42 in the abstract and table, 40 in the conclusion) and at least one apparent malformed percentage in Table VIII.
record.rows_left_out: Table IX CyberMetric results for the 80-, 500-, and 2,000-question sets were left out to stay within the 60-row limit, retaining the 10,000-question result for each listed model. Table VIII’s Qwen2-4b-instruct hardware bug-detection result (0.576%) was also left out to retain the reported zero-result models and stay within the limit. The separate per-CWE yes/no entries in Table VIII were not extracted.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss, power-law form, bottleneck controls, and orders-of-magnitude range.
Prediction of substantially larger runs from small-run fits.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their scaling exponents.
Architecture effects at fixed parameter count under comparable training.
Power-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
Quantitative prediction or extrapolation of downstream performance; relationships with pretraining loss, training tokens, or compute; controlled attribution of differences to scale.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and bending of fitted curves.

record.verdict_notes: Use Table IX's GPT-4o identity rather than the prose's GPT-4 name. Question-set size is evaluation sample count, not training-data scale. Declared omissions need no missing entries. Hardware percentage precision is difficult to reconcile with exactly 10,000 binary-scored samples, so denominators or aggregation require clarification. For r60, the sole subject correction is from the record's Starcoder2 misidentification 'Starcoder2' rendered as 'Starcoder2' to the source's exact Starcoder2-15b-instruct; the record actually names Starcoder2's different model family as Starcoder2 only through an extraction inconsistency.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law fit and range.
Extrapolation from smaller runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their trends with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities and training regimes.

The evaluations concern cybersecurity knowledge and hardware bug detection, not broad downstream task performance or a controlled relationship with pretraining loss. Model sizes and training setups are not controlled as a scaling sweep.
The paper does not test how scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits change with fitting choices, nor whether fitted curves bend.

relationships.condition: CyberMetric 10,000 questions: within-family size comparisons for Qwen1.5, base Gemma, Flan-T5, and Yi-1.5-Chat
relationships.reason: Directional improvements accompany larger size: Qwen1.5 40.29→59.79→69.96% (r33/r18/r19), Gemma 19.18→34.28% (r38/r30), Flan-T5 47.09→67.50% (r26/r12), and Yi 74.84→76.04% (r15/r07). Predictive calibration remains untested.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased from 40.29% to 59.79% to 69.96% for Qwen1.5, from 19.18% to 34.28% for Gemma, from 47.09% to 67.50% for Flan-T5, and from 74.84% to 76.04% for Yi.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: CyberMetric 10,000 questions: within-family size comparisons for Qwen1.5, base Gemma, Flan-T5, and Yi-1.5-Chat
source_check.reason: This combined group mixes substantial directional improvements for Qwen1.5 (r33/r18/r19), Gemma (r38/r30), and Flan-T5 (r26/r12) with only a small improvement for Yi, 74.84% to 76.04% (r15/r07), which the state rules classify as partial. Split the group: retain supports for the first three families and limits_scope for the small Yi effect. Predictive calibration remains untested.

relationships.condition: CyberMetric comparisons across different model families and adaptation regimes
relationships.reason: Size alone does not reliably rank these heterogeneous models: 70B Llama 2 scores 66.10% (r17), below 9B Yi at 76.04% (r07), while 16B Deepseek-MoE scores 48.76% (r27). These qualify cross-model prediction, without establishing failure of controlled scaling.
relationships.display_finding: Yi 9B scored 76.04%, above Llama 2 70B at 66.10% and Deepseek-MoE 16B at 48.76%, across differing families and adaptation regimes.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: CyberMetric comparisons across different model families and adaptation regimes
source_check.reason: Table IX confirms 70B Llama 2 at 66.10% (r17), 9B Yi at 76.04% (r07), and 16B Deepseek-MoE at 48.76% (r27). The authors explicitly report that larger models do not always perform better; heterogeneous training and architectures qualify size-only ranking.
